history.heading: Island sultanate
paragraphs: The Maldives, a chain of about 1,200 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls in the Indian Ocean, were settled by people from South Asia, including Sri Lanka and southern India. Buddhism was practised until 1153, when, according to tradition, the king converted to Islam, and the Maldives became a sultanate.

The islands were a stop on Indian Ocean trade routes and exported cowrie shells, used as currency across Africa and Asia. The Portuguese briefly occupied Malé in the 16th century until they were expelled by Muhammad Thakurufaanu, a national hero.

history.heading: Independence and democracy
paragraphs: The Maldives became a British protectorate in 1887 while keeping internal self-government, and became fully independent on 26 July 1965. The sultanate was abolished in 1968. Maumoon Abdul Gayoom ruled from 1978 to 2008.
The first multiparty elections in 2008 brought Mohamed Nasheed to power; he resigned under pressure in 2012. Politics has since been turbulent. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami caused major damage.

culture.heading: Island life
paragraphs: Dhivehi, an Indo-Aryan language with its own Thaana script, is the national language. Islam is the state religion, and citizenship requires being Muslim. Bodu beru, drumming and dance, is a traditional performance.
Fish, especially tuna, rice and coconut form the basis of the diet; mas huni (tuna with coconut and onion) is a typical breakfast.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: The Maldives is a presidential republic. Mohamed Muizzu was elected in 2023, and his party won a large parliamentary majority in 2024. Foreign policy balances relations with India, the traditional partner, and China.
As the world's lowest-lying country, the Maldives has been a leading voice on climate change; most of its land is less than a metre above sea level.

economy.heading: Luxury tourism
paragraphs: Tourism dominates the economy, with luxury "one island, one resort" hotels drawing visitors from around the world. Fishing, especially pole-and-line tuna, is the second industry.
The Maldives has achieved middle-income status but faces high public debt and dependence on imports. The currency is the rufiyaa.
